[00:00] In this lecture, we are going to go over the step-by-step procedure to create a professional price analysis. Keep in mind that this is only the general way in which things are done, and this step-by-step procedure certainly doesn't exhaust all the possibilities, details, and challenges you will find on a daily basis in any market. As I said in the beginning of this course, we are only dealing with the theory in this first installment. The true understanding of this step-by-step procedure will come with your exposure to the practical applications of the whole theory that will come in future installments. So please keep that in the back of your mind while we go through the steps.
[00:45] Step one: choosing a market. Select one market to trade. By restricting the amount of information you deal with, you can analyze this information more profoundly, and therefore, see details on it that most people simply gloss over. If you trade higher timeframes, you can select more markets because there is a lot of time to analyze things. For lower timeframes you should choose just one market.
[01:12] Step two: choosing a timeframe. Select one timeframe to trade and stick to it without checking other timeframes to get more information. Again, this is the same principle of the previous step. When you jump around between timeframes, you increase the amount of information you have to deal with, and therefore, you decrease the quality of your analysis. Don't worry, everything you need to make a good analysis is already in your timeframe of choice.
[01:41] Step three: choosing the amount of price to be analyzed. Choose the amount of price information you are going to analyze. As a rule of thumb, the relevant price information dwells around the last 100-200 candles. If you are scrolling too far back in the past, you are wasting your time because the more price information you analyze, the more complicated it gets. On the other hand, you cannot zoom in too much as well because you will have no context for your analysis.
[02:12] In this image, you can see an example of a chart that is too zoomed out. There is too much going on. We cannot see the nuances on candles. There are several types of flows and the counterpoint between market players is too complex. This chart would be a bad starting point for any analysis.
[02:33] On the other hand, if your chart looks like this at the starting point of your analysis, you will have trouble too. The chart is too zoomed in, so you don't have enough information to form a contextual analysis.
[02:48] In this third chart, you can see an optimal place to start. The chart is not too zoomed out, nor too zoomed in. There is enough information to see the nuances of price and to detect the overall context of what's going on.
[03:04] Step four: counting the major price extremes. Start counting the major price extremes. At this point, this should be a 'loose' count. Observe which price extremes are solid and which ones are fake. In this image, we can see a loose major count with the identification of solid highs in this case.
[03:25] Step five: counting the minor price extremes. Start counting the minor price extremes. Observe which price extremes are solid and which ones are fake. In this image, we can see one possible count for the minor market extremes with the identification of solid and fake structures.
[03:44] Step six: Identify the last major and minor supply and demand zones. In this image, we can see the major supply and demand zones in green and the minor supply and demand zones in red.
[03:58] Step seven: Identify the major and minor trends. Higher highs and higher lows mean uptrend. Lower highs and lower lows mean downtrend. In this image, we can see that the major flow is going down and the minor flow is going up. We can already identify an important event where the last major supply zone was broken by the minor flow, which could mean a change in the trend.
[04:22] Step eight: Identify the types of flow and the type of counterpoint between major and minor flows. We can notice that both major and minor flows appear to be displaying a traveling motion. And the counterpoint between flows seems to be classified as contrary motion because the major is going down and the minor is going up. However, since a major supply zone was disproved recently, the counterpoint between players might have changed from contrary motion to similar motion.
[04:52] Step nine: Scan the chart for the praxeological elements. Do this only for the most relevant information at the time. You can also zoom in the chart to the relevant areas by now. In this image, you can see that we have praxeological elements that point to two different ideas. One idea is a manipulation to the downside by considering the organized behaviors in the chart in combination with high volatility. And the other is a trade to the upside by the shifting quality in the last major supply zone that was broken.
[05:26] Step ten: Identify the optimal buying and selling areas. The optimal areas for buying or selling are in the last supply and demand zones, but it's not clear which one we should use.
[05:40] Step eleven: Draw the line work with all principles and techniques in mind. Remember to try finding lines that point to our relevant areas of interest. In this image, we can see some very simple line work. The idea here is for you to perceive the reverse engineering aspect of the analysis. Notice that we are looking for lines that intersect the areas of interest found by the last supply and demand zones. We don't start the analysis by drawing lines because that will become too ambiguous and confusing.
[06:11] Step twelve: Metaphysical verification for both possible trades. The Buy Trade: Despite the fact that there are many market maker elements in the chart that might lead to a sell trade as explained below, we also have the fact that the major supply zone (2) might have turned into a minor demand zone. This would be a classic example of flow shift where the minor players win over the major. The pressure bar 7, which shows selling pressure, appears to render (6) as a fake structure. However, since we are talking about minor vectors, this apparently fake structure might be a solid structure in a lower timeframe. A buy trade could be taken at the lower simple line extrapolation in black, correlating with the latest minor demand zone, assuming that (6) is not a fake structure.
[07:00] The Sell Trade: From the Hybrid Bar (3), and the Organized Behavior in (4), we can sense that there might be market makers in this market. Even though the major supply zone (2) created a bump down, the market broke it to the upside with another display of Organized Behavior (5). Market makers might be washing the line coming out of 1, which would not be a surprise given the amount of market makers elements in the analysis. A possible sell trade would be at the upper line of the blue fork, possibly correlating with the wash line too.
[07:34] Notice that this analysis is very different than simply noticing a setup appear and pulling the trigger out of mere blind impulse. Observe how there is a whole narrative implied in the analysis. Identifying this narrative should be your ultimate goal as a trader. Remember, the metaphysical verification is trying to explain the causal relationship between facts in the chart. Listing facts is not enough. We must find a causal connection between them.
[08:03] So, which trade do we take? We can take both in this case. Since we are observing the edges of both sides of the market, when we are not sure about the direction, we can play both sides and usually one of them will win. By using a good risk-reward ratio, the profit from one will be larger than the loss of the other. This is an aspect of game theory that helps us eliminate some of the subjectivity out of the situation.
[08:32] Some time later, we can see the aftermath of the whole situation where the shift in the major supply zone to major demand zone intersected with the creation of a minor demand zone. In other words, the buy trade would be correct and the sell trade would be wrong. The important aspect here is that by placing the stop loss at the correct places, we would get out of the sell trade with a small loss and out of the buy trade with a profit about three times as big. It's very difficult to encapsulate all the details of a general analysis in one presentation like this, but I wanted to create it to give you an overall idea of how this happens. There are details in here that I haven't talked about because they were too peculiar to this analysis. So once again, keep in mind that you will only learn how to do this by getting exposed to several types of analysis that will go much deeper in detail than this one. This is just a general framework for you to have in mind.

Text on the chart reads: 'Too much price information: 1) We can barely see the nuances on candles. 2) Too much going on. 3) Several types of flow happening. 4) Counterpoint between players is too complex.'

A candlestick chart for FX:EURUSD on a 120-minute timeframe is displayed. The chart is extremely zoomed in, showing only a handful of very large candles. Text on the chart reads: 'Not enough price information: 1) No context for trades. 2) Not enough counterpoint between players.'

A candlestick chart for FX:EURUSD on a 120-minute timeframe is displayed, showing an optimal amount of data (approx. 100-200 candles). Text on the chart reads: 'Optimal amount of price information: 1) Not too much. Not too little. 2) Zoomed out enough to see the big picture. 3) Zoomed in enough to see candle nuances.'

Slide with a translucent green rectangle over the Aristotle bust. Title: 'Step 4:'. Body: 'Start counting the major price extremes. At this point this should be a "loose" count. Observe which price extremes are solid and which ones are fake.'
The optimal chart from 02:49 is shown. Major swing highs and lows are marked with translucent blue circles. Four of the major swing highs are labeled with the text 'Solid'.
Slide with a translucent green rectangle. Title: 'Step 5:'. Body: 'Start counting the minor price extremes. Observe which price extremes are solid and which ones are fake.'
The chart from 03:18 is shown. In addition to the blue circles (major extremes), numerous minor swing highs and lows are now marked with translucent red circles. One minor low is labeled 'Fake'.
Slide with a translucent green rectangle. Title: 'Step 6:'. Body: 'Identify the last major and minor supply and demand zones'.

The fully annotated chart from 03:36 is shown. Now, horizontal zones are drawn. Two green rectangles are labeled 'Major Supply Zone'. Two red rectangles are labeled 'Minor Demand Zone' and 'Minor Demand Zone?'.
Slide with a translucent green rectangle. Title: 'Step 7:'. Body: 'Identify the major and minor trends. Higher highs and higher lows mean uptrend. Lower highs and lower lows mean down trend.'

The chart with all previous annotations is shown. New text is added: 'Major Flow is going down. Minor Flow is going up. However, the last major solid structure has just been broken by the minor flow going up'. Arrows visually indicate the direction of the major and minor flows.
Slide with a translucent green rectangle. Title: 'Step 8:'. Body: 'Identify the types of flow and the type of counterpoint between major and minor flows.'

The chart with all previous annotations is shown. New text is added at the bottom left: 'Both Major and Minor flows appear to be displaying a Travelling Flow. Major and Minor flows are in Contrary Motion (One is going up and the other is going down).'

Slide with a translucent green rectangle. Title: 'Step 9:'. Body: 'Scan the chart for the praxeological elements. Do this only for the most relevant information at the time. You can also zoom in the chart to the relevant points by now.'

The chart is re-displayed with numbers 1 through 7 pointing to specific events. A text box lists what each number represents: '1 - Frequency line that appears to be relevant at 7. 2 - Major supply zone. 3 - Hybrid Bar (Fractal+Outside+Pressure). 4 - Organized Behavior. 5 - Organized Behavior. 6 - Major Supply Zone was broken. It could turn into a Minor Demand Zone (maybe a Flow Shift). 7 - Pressure Bar (Selling Pressure)'.
Slide with a translucent green rectangle. Title: 'Step 10:'. Body: 'Identify the optimal buying and selling areas.'

The chart is re-displayed with all previous annotations. A new text box at the bottom summarizes potential trades: '- 6 could be a good place to buy if the major supply zone has indeed turned into a minor demand zone. The lower minor demand zone could also be an interesting place to buy. - A good place to sell would be the highest major supply zone in the chart, but that's a bit far away for now. The selling possibility here would be a market manipulation maneuver that might have already occured in candle 7.'

Slide with a translucent green rectangle. Title: 'Step 11:'. Body: 'Draw the line work with all the principles and techniques in mind. Remember to try finding lines that point to the our relevant areas of interest.'

The fully analyzed chart is shown with new line work. A blue channel (fork) is drawn around the recent uptrending minor flow. A simple black trendline is extrapolated from the recent lows. Text is added: 'Upper blue fork parallel for sell? Lower simple line extrapolation for buy?'
Slide with a translucent green rectangle. Title: 'Step 12:'. Body: 'Metaphysical Verification for both possible trades.'

A slide with a green text box at the top, explaining the rationale for a buy trade, and a red box at the bottom (revealed at 07:00), explaining the rationale for a sell trade. Both texts are transcribed in the 'fullTranscription' section.

Slide with a solid green rectangle. Text reads: 'Notice that this analysis is VERY different than simply noticing a setup appear and pulling the trigger out of mere blind impulse. Observe how there is a whole narrative implied in the analysis. Identifying this narrative should be your ultimate goal as a trader. REMEMBER: The Metaphysical Verification is trying to explain how facts progress in the chart. Listing facts is not enough!'
Slide with a translucent green rectangle. Text reads: 'So, which trade do we take?'

Slide with a solid green rectangle. Text reads: 'We can take BOTH. Since we are observing the edges of both sides of the market, when we are not sure about the direction, we can play both sides, and usually one of them will win. By using a good risk reward ratio, the profit from one will be larger than the loss of the other. This is an aspect of game theory that helps us eliminate some of the subjectivity out of the situation.'

A new chart shows the price action following the analysis. Price has moved significantly upward, confirming the buy trade scenario. A text box on the chart reads: 'We can see that the manipulation trade was wrong, and the flow shift trade to the upside was correct.'

semanticAnalysis.mainConcept: The core concept is a 12-step systematic process for conducting a professional price analysis. This methodology moves beyond simple pattern recognition by integrating concepts like major/minor market flows, supply and demand zones, solid vs. fake structures, and praxeological elements (like organized behavior and pressure bars). The final and most crucial step is 'Metaphysical Verification,' which involves constructing a causal narrative that explains *how* and *why* price is moving, rather than just listing observed facts.
semanticAnalysis.deeperMeaning: The video implies that successful trading is not about finding 'setups' but about understanding the underlying market narrative and the dynamic interplay between different market participants (major vs. minor players). The emphasis on restricting information (one market, one timeframe) suggests that depth of analysis is superior to breadth. The introduction of 'Metaphysical Verification' and game theory (taking both sides of a trade when uncertain) elevates the trading process from a purely technical exercise to a strategic and philosophical one, focused on managing uncertainty and risk by understanding the causal logic of the market.
semanticAnalysis.educationalGoal: The educational objective is to provide traders with a structured, comprehensive, and repeatable framework for market analysis. It aims to shift the trader's mindset from being a reactive pattern-follower to a proactive analyst who builds a logical, evidence-based case for potential market direction. This 'Step by Step Analysis' serves as a foundational blueprint for developing a deep, nuanced understanding of price action, forming the basis for more advanced trading decisions.
